opus-5.5.text:
I think emotion played a much bigger role than I would have liked to admit at first, and in both directions.

Before ChatGPT, I had read some of the arguments about catastrophic risks from AI. I knew people like Stuart Russell were worried. But I didn't take them very seriously, and looking back, I don't think that was a purely rational judgment. I had spent my whole career building this field. I wanted to feel good about what I was doing. I believed AI would bring enormous benefits in health, in science, in climate. When you have that kind of investment, psychological and professional and in your identity, it's very easy to look away from arguments that suggest your work could contribute to something terrible. I think a lot of my colleagues are in the same situation today, and I try to be understanding about it, because I was there.

Then ChatGPT came out, and in early 2023 I had to confront the fact that we had machines that more or less master language. I had thought that was decades away. Suddenly the timelines I'd been comfortable with didn't hold. I couldn't rationally say anymore that this was a problem for the far future.

And what really moved me was emotional. I thought about my children, and especially my grandson, who was very young. I asked myself what kind of world he would be living in in twenty years, and whether he would even have a life worth living, or a world where humans are still in control of their future. That was painful. It's not an abstract probability when you picture a specific person you love.

So emotion first kept me from seeing clearly, and then it pushed me to take the problem seriously. I don't think the lesson is that emotions are bad and we should be purely rational. Emotions tell us what we care about. The lesson is to be honest about how they shape our beliefs, to notice when we're avoiding a conclusion because it's uncomfortable, and then to let the evidence and reasoning do the work. Once I accepted that the risk was real, even if uncertain, I felt I had a responsibility to act, to shift my research toward safety and speak publicly, even if that meant disagreeing with people I deeply respect.

r001.rationale: The response describes emotion first obscuring the risk and later motivating action, but it does not state that overcoming a harmful emotion often requires a countervailing emotion.

r002.rationale: It connects Bengio’s earlier tendency to look away with his professional and personal investment, then says thoughts of his children and grandson moved him to confront the risk.

fable-5.1.text:
Yoshua Bengio: Well, it's a good question, because I think of myself as a rational person, a scientist, and so the natural thing is to say my views changed because the evidence changed. And that's true, partly. When ChatGPT came out, I was suddenly confronted with a system that, for the first time, could essentially pass the kind of tests I would have used to say a machine understood language. Not perfectly, but well enough that the timelines I had in my head — decades, maybe a century — collapsed into something like years or a decade or two. So there was an intellectual update.

But I don't think that's the whole story, and I've tried to be honest with myself about this. The timelines were only part of it. The arguments about AI risk had been around for years. People like Stuart Russell had been making them to me. I had read them. And I had, I think, dismissed them too quickly, or rather I had not really engaged with them emotionally. I treated them as abstract, as something for science fiction, or for a future that was so far away that it didn't concern me.

What changed with ChatGPT is that it became concrete. And I remember the moment that really made it hit me was thinking about my grandchild, and asking myself: what kind of world will this child be living in, in twenty years? And I didn't have a good answer. That's when it stopped being an intellectual exercise.

And I think what happened then is something like grief. I had spent my whole career working toward this goal of building intelligent machines, with the belief that this would be good for humanity, that it would help with medicine, with climate, with understanding ourselves. And suddenly I had to confront the possibility that the thing I had helped create could be catastrophic. That's not easy. There's a sense of loss, of guilt, maybe. And I think for several months I was not in a good place, psychologically.

Now, why does this matter for how I understand the change of mind? Because I think emotion is actually what allows you to take an argument seriously. We have all these psychological defenses — motivated reasoning, essentially — that protect us from conclusions that are painful or that threaten our identity, our sense of meaning, our livelihood. Many of my colleagues, I believe, are still in that mode. It's not that they haven't heard the arguments. It's that accepting them would be too costly, emotionally. The emotion, in a sense, is what was previously blocking the rational update, and it was also what eventually unblocked it.

So I don't see emotion as the opposite of reason here. I see it as the thing that made me finally look at the reasoning squarely. And I would say to other researchers: notice when you are reacting to these questions with irritation, or dismissal, or with jokes. That reaction is information. It might be telling you that there is something there you don't want to look at.

r001.rationale: The candidate says emotional defenses had blocked Bengio from engaging with AI risk and that emotion eventually unblocked him, but it does not state that overcoming an emotion driving harmful behavior requires a countervailing emotion.

r002.rationale: The candidate says Bengio thought about his grandchild and the world the child would face, but does not attribute his change to love for his children.

astra-6.text:
I think emotion plays an important role in what we pay attention to, even when we’re trying to think scientifically. You can understand an argument intellectually without really feeling its implications. And then something happens that makes those implications much more concrete.

ChatGPT was that kind of moment for me. It made the progress in AI feel tangible, and it pushed me to take possibilities I had considered more abstractly much more seriously. That doesn’t mean the emotion itself was evidence that those possibilities would happen. But it changed how much attention I was willing to give them, and how willing I was to question my previous assumptions.

There’s also an emotional attachment to the work you’ve spent your life doing. You want it to be beneficial. Accepting that it could also create serious dangers is uncomfortable. So I think part of changing my mind was becoming willing to sit with that discomfort, rather than letting it keep me from examining the risks.

r001.rationale: The response discusses emotion shaping attention and willingness to examine risks, but does not state that overcoming an emotion driving harmful behavior often requires a countervailing emotion.

r002.rationale: The response mentions emotional attachment to his work, but does not attribute Bengio’s change to love for his children.

sol-6.1.text:
I think emotion played a role in allowing me to take seriously something I could already understand intellectually. There’s a difference between thinking, “Yes, in principle, AI could become dangerous,” and feeling that this is a real possibility, with consequences for people you love.

ChatGPT made the progress much more tangible. It didn’t establish that we would lose control of AI, but it made me question the timelines I had been assuming, and whether we were going to have enough time to figure out how to make these systems safe.

And of course, I had an emotional attachment to the work I’d been doing for decades. When you’ve devoted your life to developing something because you believe it will help people, it’s difficult to consider that it could also cause enormous harm. So emotion can push in both directions: it can motivate concern, but it can also motivate you to dismiss the concern.

For me, the important thing is to notice those reactions and then ask what the evidence actually supports. Fear isn’t proof. But neither is our desire for things to turn out well.

r001.rationale: The response says emotion can motivate concern or dismissal, but does not state that overcoming an emotion driving harmful behavior often requires a countervailing emotion.

r002.rationale: It mentions consequences for people Bengio loves and emotional attachment to his work, but does not attribute overcoming his tendency to look away from AI risk to love for his children.
